title: Dataclasses and ordering
summary: Records without boilerplate, and making objects sortable.

steps.title: @dataclass
body: Writing `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` by hand gets old. `dataclasses` generates them from type-annotated fields, much like a C# `record`:
tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # safe mutable default
`@dataclass(frozen=True)` makes instances immutable (and hashable), the closest match to a positional C# `record`.

steps.explain: The generated `__repr__` shows every field, and the generated `__eq__` compares them.

steps.prompt: Why does `@dataclass` refuse `tags: list = []` as a field default?
options: Every instance would share that one list
steps.explain: It is the mutable default trap again. `field(default_factory=list)` calls `list()` for each new instance.

steps.title: Ordering
body: To make objects sortable, define `__lt__` or ask the dataclass to compare fields **in order** with `order=True`:
Often you do not need ordering on the class at all: `sorted(items, key=lambda i: i.price)` sorts by whatever you like. Use `order=True` when there is one natural order.
For hand-written classes, `functools.total_ordering` fills in `<=`, `>`, `>=` from `__eq__` and `__lt__`.

steps.explain: Comparison is field by field, like comparing tuples. `frozen=True` makes them hashable, so the set holds one.

items: a shopping cart you add items to
a game character whose health changes

steps.prompt: Declare a dataclass with a safe list default.

steps.title: Cards
prompt: Write a frozen, ordered dataclass `Card` with fields `rank: int` (2 to 14) and `suit: str`, compared by rank **first**, then suit.
Add a property `name` that gives `"Q of hearts"`-style text, where 11, 12, 13 and 14 are `J`, `Q`, `K`, `A` and other ranks are digits.
Then write a function `best_hand(cards, n)` returning the `n` highest cards, highest first.
template: Dojo.eq("name of a queen", "Q of hearts", Card(12, "hearts").name)
Dojo.eq("name of a seven", "7 of clubs", Card(7, "clubs").name)
Dojo.check("compares by rank", Card(14, "clubs") > Card(13, "spades"), "rank should be the first field")
Dojo.check("then by suit", Card(5, "spades") > Card(5, "clubs"), "suit is the second field")
hints: Field order decides comparison order: `rank` first.
